chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarak, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Aasim ibn Humayd, from Abu Hamza, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him, 'May I be sacrificed for you, what do you say regarding a Muslim who visits another Muslim or seeks a need while he is in his house, so he seeks permission from him, but he does not grant him permission and does not come out to him?'

He said, 'O Abu Hamza! Whichever Muslim visits another Muslim or seeks a need while he is in his house, so he seeks permission from him and he does not come out to him, he will not cease to be in the Curse of Allah until they both meet.'
So I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you, (is he) in the Curse of Allah until they both meet?' He said, 'Yes, O Abu Hamza.'
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence for a Muslim who refuses entry to a visiting brother seeking a need?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this narration from Imam al-Baqir (AS) to highlight the severity of obstructing a brother's visit or request for need. The Imam specifies that the host remains under the 'Curse of Allah' (La'nat Allah) until the two parties finally meet, emphasizing that mere refusal without a valid excuse constitutes a grave spiritual defect. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on social connectivity and the obligation of hospitality within the community of believers.
